title: The case against adoption
gist: On the centenary of the 1926 Adoption of Children Act, adoptee and investigative journalist Katharine Quarmby surveys the coercive 'baby scoop' era (1949-1976), transracial 'colour watching', international inquiries into adoption abuses, and register evidence (notably Sweden's) of elevated adult psychiatric and suicide risk among adoptees, arguing adoptee voices now drive a reckoning that favours kinship care and family support; her own survey finds 90% of adult adoptees lack adjusted family-history risk assessment in healthcare.

themes.theme: Scale and coercion of the UK 'baby scoop' era

insights.claim: Historian Michael Lambert estimates that of around 500,000 babies adopted across the UK between 1949 and 1976, some 185,000 to 215,000 were adoptions with no relative of the child involved.
insights.speaker: Katharine Quarmby
insights.so_what: Quantifies the cohort affected by historic forced adoption, relevant to potential redress or compensation schemes.

insights.claim: Close to a million people are estimated to have been adopted in England and Wales since 1949, with fully half of those adoptions occurring in the 1949-1976 peak period now defined as a framework of coercive adoption.
insights.speaker: Katharine Quarmby
insights.so_what: A large, ageing population with unmet health and identity needs shapes NHS and social policy demand.

themes.theme: Outcomes evidence: adoptees' elevated adult risks

insights.claim: Mid-20th-century studies reporting positive adoption outcomes focused on babies placed in stable families with small samples, and a 2023 CoramBaaf review acknowledged a limited knowledge base on adoption outcomes.
insights.speaker: Katharine Quarmby
insights.so_what: Weak evidence base undermines the 'gold standard' claim for adoption in policy.

insights.so_what: Lifelong elevated risks imply higher long-run health and welfare costs than child-focused outcome metrics capture.

themes.theme: Global inquiries and the 'era of reckoning'

insights.claim: Inquiries in Ireland, Northern Ireland, Australia, the Netherlands, Scandinavia and South Korea have uncovered coercion, fraud and falsified documents in adoption; the Netherlands' Joustra Commission led to a suspension of intercountry adoption in 2021.
insights.speaker: Katharine Quarmby
insights.so_what: Intercountry adoption is contracting globally under regulatory scrutiny.

insights.claim: Hübinette says adoption has entered 'the era of reckoning and reconciliation', with self-advocacy groups such as the Adult Adoptee Movement and How to be Adopted emerging worldwide.
insights.speaker: Katharine Quarmby
insights.so_what: Organised adoptee advocacy increases pressure for apologies, redress and policy reform.

themes.theme: Healthcare blind spot for adult adoptees

insights.claim: In Quarmby's 2026 survey of 206 UK adult adoptees, 90% said clinicians assumed 'no relevant family history' or recorded 'unknown' without adjusting risk assessment, and only 6% had a full family health history even after reunion.
insights.speaker: Katharine Quarmby
insights.so_what: Missing family history creates demand for DNA testing and genetic screening among adoptees.
